Adamant

/AD-uh-ment/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Adamant means refusing to be persuaded or to change one's mind; unyielding.

Adamant means refusing to be persuaded or to change one's mind; unyielding. Dad was adamant that the tent be pitched before dark, no matter how much we wanted to swim first.

Worked Example

The band's producer wanted to cut the seven-minute song down to radio length. The label sent charts showing that shorter singles streamed better. Even the drummer suggested trimming a verse. Through every meeting, the lead singer was adamant: the song would run seven minutes or it would not be released at all. She said it plainly, said it loudly, and never budged an inch.

The singer's loud, repeated, emphatic insistence on one specific point — the song's full length — despite pressure from every side is what makes her adamant.

How Adamant Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

insistent

insistent: demanding firmly and repeatedly

Antonyms

yielding

yielding: giving way to others

persuadable

persuadable: open to being convinced

How Strong Is It? — firm → unshakable → adamant

firm vs. adamant

firm vs. adamant: Firm is milder — a firm person holds a position calmly but can still be talked around with a good enough argument; an adamant one announces that no argument will work.

unshakable vs. adamant

unshakable vs. adamant: Unshakable is stronger than adamant: it rules out even the possibility of doubt, while adamant describes the emphatic refusal itself.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — a-

Prefix — a-: not (Greek)

Root — damant

Root — damant: to tame, to conquer (Greek daman)

Put it together

Put it together: Adamant comes from Greek adamas, 'untamable': a- (not) plus daman (to tame). The Greeks used adamas as the name of the hardest imaginable substance, and that word traveled into English twice — once as adamant, the unpersuadable temperament, and once, through Old French, as diamond, the unscratchable stone. Both are things nothing can cut.

Use the root in a new word: diamond

Use the root in a new word: diamond: A diamond can scratch every other stone — diamond is literally the same word as Greek adamas, 'the untamable one,' which is why an adamant person is as hard to move as the hardest stone on earth.
